name: Cans/lids
anchor: EU food-contact framework Regulation 1935/2004 with Regulation (EU) 10/2011 Annex II specific migration limits as the only element-migration instrument in the register; polymer-surface rows anchor it directly or by disclosed read-across, and metal, alloy, ceramic-glaze, vitreous-enamel and glass rows are controls because their dedicated release regimes are not yet ingested.
cross_reference: Category 9 (Infant and Child Contact Products) governs any article in this row that is marketed for ages 0-5; the taxonomy boundary rule routes infant bottles, nipples and toddler drinkware there even though they are food-contact items.
native_basis: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food), Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II convention
native_basis_label: specific element migration INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT from the polymeric food-contact surface, µg/kg of food, determined by the Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex III to V simulant, temperature and contact-time conventions. This is a MIGRATION basis and not a total-content basis: no cell on this row limits how much of an element the material CONTAINS, and no cell on this row is expressed per kg of material.
scope_note: The finished sealed can and its end as filled and processed, including hot-fill and retort sterilised product. The food-contact surface of a modern food can is the cured organic interior lacquer, so the published ceilings read across from the plastics migration instrument. Where a can interior is UNCOATED tinplate, or where the lacquer is breached, that configuration falls to the metal-article release control regime instead, and the tin cell is a control on every configuration. Tin is the defining pathway for this row and the canned-food tin maximum levels are a FOOD-basis companion on the contents, disclosed here and never published as this row's migration ceiling.
basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as specific element migration into food or a food simulant may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap.
method: HMTc Method v2.0 (government-limit-only): the strictest applicable sovereign maximum for this exact product form expressed as specific element migration into food or a food simulant; a disclosed read-across from the nearest applicable sovereign value in the same basis where the food-contact material family is expressly excluded from or not reached by that instrument; a substantiated not-material determination; or a control. No cell is occurrence-derived, and no cell borrows a value across a basis.

Pb.basis: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
Pb.label: read-across of the EU 10/2011 Annex II point 2 lead non-detect requirement (0.01 mg/kg food)
Pb.substantiation: The exact cell is unregulated: the food-contact surface of a food can is a cured organic coating, and coatings and varnishes are a Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, while Regulation (EU) 10/2011 reaches plastic layers and plastic coatings in multi-material multi-layer articles but is not written for a liquid-applied cured lacquer. The nearest applicable sovereign value in the identical basis is therefore the EU 10/2011 Annex II element requirement for a polymeric food-contact layer, and it is read across with disclosure. The read-across holds the basis constant: source and destination are the same measured quantity, specific element migration into food or a food simulant in µg/kg food, determined by the same test conventions. The analogy is on basis and exposure endpoint, not on material identity, and it is disclosed as a read-across rather than presented as a limit written for this article. Lead is on the Annex II point 2 not-detectable list, so the published ceiling is the 0.01 mg/kg food detection limit and not a positive migration allowance. Applied to the can, this ceiling governs the lacquered interior surface as the food-contact surface; the uncoated-tinplate and breached-coating configurations are handled by the component plan under the metal-article release control regime, and the tin pathway is a control on every configuration. This is a migration ceiling on the food or simulant and is never reported as a limit on the material's lead content; the material-content instruments (US CPSIA total lead in children's-product substrate, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS 2024-29 percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals and solder) are separate obligations in a different basis and are not this cell.

tAs.basis: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
tAs.label: read-across of the EU 10/2011 Annex II point 2 total-arsenic non-detect requirement (0.01 mg/kg food)
tAs.substantiation: The exact cell is unregulated: the food-contact surface of a food can is a cured organic coating, and coatings and varnishes are a Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, while Regulation (EU) 10/2011 reaches plastic layers and plastic coatings in multi-material multi-layer articles but is not written for a liquid-applied cured lacquer. The read-across holds the basis constant: source and destination are the same measured quantity, specific element migration into food or a food simulant in µg/kg food, determined by the same test conventions. The analogy is on basis and exposure endpoint, not on material identity, and it is disclosed as a read-across rather than presented as a limit written for this article. Arsenic is on the Annex II point 2 not-detectable list and the instrument states it as the total element, so this cell is total arsenic and cannot be satisfied by an inorganic-arsenic determination. iAs.rationale: Inorganic arsenic is a dietary speciation with no separate food-contact-material instrument anywhere in the credible set: every food-contact element requirement is written on total arsenic. Arsenic migrating from a polymeric food-contact article is in any case inorganic, so the total-arsenic non-detect requirement is simultaneously the tightest achievable inorganic-arsenic ceiling and bounds this cell by identity. No separate inorganic-arsenic ceiling is published, and inorganic arsenic never substitutes for the total-arsenic cell.
iAs.reference_method: Total-arsenic migration determination per the tAs cell; reflex inorganic-arsenic speciation by HPLC-ICP-MS on the migration extract only where total arsenic is detected at or above the detection limit.
iAs.bounded_by: tAs (read-across of eu_10_2011_tas_sml_nd, total arsenic not detectable at 0.01 mg/kg food)
iAs.regulatory_basis: Regulation (EU) 10/2011 Annex II point 2 sets the element requirement as a specific migration requirement on the food or food simulant, not as a limit on the material's element content. No credible sovereign sets a species-specific migration limit for this cell.
iAs.jurisdictions_checked: EU (Reg (EU) 1935/2004 framework + Annex I material families; Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II element list, as amended by 2016/1416 and 2020/1245); UK (retained Reg 10/2011); US (FDA food-contact substances, 21 CFR 174-190: no element migration ceiling for these elements); Codex (no food-contact-material standard); AU-NZ (FSANZ Food Standards Code 1.4.3 and 3.2.2: no element migration ceiling); Canada (Food and Drugs Act s.4 / letter-of-no-objection route, no numeric element migration ceiling); Hong Kong (Cap 132 subsidiary legislation: food limits only).

MeHg.rationale: Methylmercury is formed by microbial methylation in aquatic food chains. A cured polymer, a fired glaze, a metal alloy and a coated article contain no methylation pathway, and no credible sovereign sets a methylmercury requirement for any food-contact material. The total-mercury non-detect requirement bounds any organomercury fraction that could be present. No separate methylmercury ceiling is published, and methylmercury never substitutes for the total-mercury cell.

Ni.basis: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
Ni.label: read-across of the EU 10/2011 Annex II point 1 nickel SML (0.02 mg/kg food)
Ni.substantiation: The exact cell is unregulated: the food-contact surface of a food can is a cured organic coating, and coatings and varnishes are a Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, while Regulation (EU) 10/2011 reaches plastic layers and plastic coatings in multi-material multi-layer articles but is not written for a liquid-applied cured lacquer. The nearest applicable sovereign value in the identical basis is therefore the EU 10/2011 Annex II element requirement for a polymeric food-contact layer, and it is read across with disclosure. The read-across holds the basis constant: source and destination are the same measured quantity, specific element migration into food or a food simulant in µg/kg food, determined by the same test conventions. The analogy is on basis and exposure endpoint, not on material identity, and it is disclosed as a read-across rather than presented as a limit written for this article. Nickel carries a positive specific migration limit of 0.02 mg/kg food, the tightest positive SML in the Annex II element list. Applied to the can, this ceiling governs the lacquered interior surface as the food-contact surface; the uncoated-tinplate and breached-coating configurations are handled by the component plan under the metal-article release control regime, and the tin pathway is a control on every configuration. This value governs the polymeric food-contact surface only; where a food-contact component of the article is a nickel-bearing alloy, that component sits in the alloy-release control regime described in this row's component plan, because the plastics SML was not written for and is not achievable by a bare stainless-steel surface.

Sn.rationale: Regulation (EU) 10/2011 Annex II lists no tin entry, and no credible sovereign sets a tin migration or release ceiling for a can, a can end or any other food-contact article. Tin is the defining pathway of this row, so a control here is a mandatory determination and not a shrug: tin dissolves from exposed tinplate wherever the interior lacquer is absent, thin or breached, which is why the sovereign response to canned-food tin is a maximum level on the FOOD rather than on the article. Those food maximum levels (EU Reg 2023/915 at 200 mg/kg for canned foods and 100 mg/kg for canned beverages, Codex CXS 193 and FSANZ Schedule 19 at 250 mg/kg, and 50 mg/kg for canned infant and young-child products) are disclosed as a companion obligation on the contents. They are a FOOD basis, they are measured in the food and not in a simulant against the article, and republishing one of them as this row's migration ceiling would be the exact basis conflation this category's guard exists to prevent.
Sn.reference_method: EN 1186 / EN 13130 food-simulant migration testing on the finished article under its worst foreseeable use conditions (simulant, temperature and contact time selected per Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex III and Annex V; for repeat-use articles the third successive migration result governs), with ICP-MS determination of the element in the simulant. Tin determined additionally on the finished packed product at the end of the declared shelf life, and on the seam and end-panel extraction separately, because tin dissolution is progressive and localised.

Cr.basis: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
Cr.label: read-across of the EU 10/2011 Annex II point 2 total-chromium non-detect requirement (0.01 mg/kg food), relaxation declined
Cr.substantiation: The exact cell is unregulated: the food-contact surface of a food can is a cured organic coating, and coatings and varnishes are a Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, while Regulation (EU) 10/2011 reaches plastic layers and plastic coatings in multi-material multi-layer articles but is not written for a liquid-applied cured lacquer. The nearest applicable sovereign value in the identical basis is therefore the EU 10/2011 Annex II element requirement for a polymeric food-contact layer, and it is read across with disclosure. The read-across holds the basis constant: source and destination are the same measured quantity, specific element migration into food or a food simulant in µg/kg food, determined by the same test conventions. The analogy is on basis and exposure endpoint, not on material identity, and it is disclosed as a read-across rather than presented as a limit written for this article. This total-chromium cell is deliberately published as a firm ceiling rather than the usual non-protective total-chromium screen, and the reason is structural to the instrument. Annex II point 2 as amended by Reg (EU) 2020/1245 sets total chromium at not detectable and permits a relaxed 3.6 mg/kg food limit only where the operator documents that chromium(VI) is absent. The non-detect branch therefore exists precisely because hexavalent chromium cannot be assumed absent, which makes it the hexavalent-chromium-conservative form of the requirement rather than a chromium(III)-dominated artefact. HMTc publishes the non-detect branch and declines the relaxation, and the hexavalent-chromium cell is bounded by this value. Applied to the can, this ceiling governs the lacquered interior surface as the food-contact surface; the uncoated-tinplate and breached-coating configurations are handled by the component plan under the metal-article release control regime, and the tin pathway is a control on every configuration.

Cr-VI.rationale: Regulation (EU) 10/2011 Annex II point 2 controls hexavalent chromium through the total-chromium requirement rather than through a separate species limit: total chromium must be not detectable, and the relaxed 3.6 mg/kg food value becomes available only where the operator documents that chromium(VI) is absent. HMTc declines that relaxation, so every certified article is held to total chromium not detectable at 0.01 mg/kg food, which bounds hexavalent chromium at or below the same value. No credible sovereign sets a hexavalent-chromium migration limit for a food-contact material, so no separate species ceiling is published; hexavalent chromium never substitutes for the total-chromium cell.
Cr-VI.reference_method: Total-chromium migration determination per the Cr cell; reflex hexavalent-chromium speciation by ion-chromatography ICP-MS on the migration extract where total chromium is detected at or above the detection limit, and on any chromate-conversion-coated or passivated food-contact component regardless of the total result.
Cr-VI.bounded_by: Cr (read-across of eu_10_2011_crtotal_sml_nd, total chromium not detectable at 0.01 mg/kg food, relaxation declined)
Cr-VI.regulatory_basis: Regulation (EU) 10/2011 Annex II point 2 sets the element requirement as a specific migration requirement on the food or food simulant, not as a limit on the material's element content. No credible sovereign sets a species-specific migration limit for this cell.
Cr-VI.jurisdictions_checked: EU (Reg (EU) 1935/2004 framework + Annex I material families; Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II element list, as amended by 2016/1416 and 2020/1245); UK (retained Reg 10/2011); US (FDA food-contact substances, 21 CFR 174-190: no element migration ceiling for these elements); Codex (no food-contact-material standard); AU-NZ (FSANZ Food Standards Code 1.4.3 and 3.2.2: no element migration ceiling); Canada (Food and Drugs Act s.4 / letter-of-no-objection route, no numeric element migration ceiling); Hong Kong (Cap 132 subsidiary legislation: food limits only).
